If you're travelling with children, Yas Mall and the theme parks make it easy to build a full day around the concert. A typical pattern is an afternoon at one of the parks, an early dinner at Yas Bay, then the arena.

- **Filming:** short clips are normal at concerts, but holding a phone up for a whole song blocks the people behind you.
- **Behaviour:** public displays of affection and rowdy drunkenness are frowned on in the UAE. Keep the energy in the singing.
- **Paying:** card and mobile payments are widely accepted across Yas Island.

On the floor, people pack in near the stage for the big dance numbers. Families with small children usually prefer seats in the tiers, where the sightlines take in the whole formation of the choreography.

Our advice is simple: don't treat Yaowarat as a single sight to tick off. Walk the road slowly, look at what the stalls and shopfronts are cooking, and let the street set the pace.

Most signage and subtitles run in Korean and English, and staff at the Busan Cinema Center's info desk switch easily between both.

For meals between screenings, the surrounding Centum City strip has fast, affordable options built for exactly this rhythm: quick Korean and Japanese chains rather than long sit-down restaurants. If you're catching multiple films across venues, budget the walk or a short taxi ride, since satellite cinemas aren't always adjacent to the Cinema Center itself.

Most big-city marathons end on an open road. Frankfurt ends indoors. The final metres run off the street and into the Festhalle, a domed exhibition hall from 1909 on the Messe grounds. Runners cross the line under lights, with a crowd packed around them on every side.

That finish is the reason many international runners pick this race. Frankfurt is Germany's longest-established city marathon and its second-largest by finishers. The 2026 edition is set for **October 25, 2026**, and it draws over 20,000 participants from around the world.

The course is flat. Frankfurt has a long-standing reputation as one of the faster marathons in the world, and elite fields have set fast times here more than once. If you are chasing a personal best in autumn, that is the attraction.
The facts that hold steady:

Start times, wave allocations, the exact route and bag-drop arrangements can change from year to year. Confirm timing and tickets on the official site. Do not rely on a route map from a previous edition.

In past years, number pick-up and the race expo have been held at the Messe on the days before the race. Check the official schedule for the pick-up window. Plan to arrive in Frankfurt by Saturday at the latest.
This date has a quirk worth knowing. October 25, 2026 is the last Sunday of October. That is the night Central Europe switches from summer time back to standard time. At 3am, clocks go back to 2am.
For runners, this is a gift: an extra hour in bed before a morning start. It is also a trap. Your phone updates itself. A hotel-room alarm clock or an older watch may not.

- Set your alarm on your phone, not the bedside clock.
- Check the race start time against the new local time, not summer time.
- If you flew in from another continent, your body clock is already confused. Write the start time down in plain numbers the night before.

For runners, the "ticket" is a race entry. You buy it through the official registration platform. Entry fees, categories and any relay or shorter-distance options are listed there, and the price is printed on the registration page. Big autumn marathons in Europe can fill up, so register early if you have your heart set on this one.
Inside the Festhalle, seating around the finish has historically been limited. Check the official site for how access works for friends and family.

Along the course, the city-centre stretches and the river crossings draw the biggest crowds. Pick two or three points on the official route map that you can link by tram or U-Bahn. That way you see your runner more than once.
What to bring:

- Warm layers. Late October in Frankfurt is usually cool, and standing still for hours feels colder than it is.
- A sign with your runner's name, large enough to read at speed.
- The live-tracking app, if the race offers one, so you know when to look up.
On race day, many roads are closed and driving across town is slow. Use the trains. Frankfurt's public transport network is run under the RMV system, and it works well for spectators.
Book a hotel near the Hauptbahnhof or the Messe and you can walk to the start. That saves you a crowded early train on race morning.

Germans take the Sunday rest day seriously. Most supermarkets and shops close on Sundays, and race day is a Sunday. Buy your breakfast, gels and post-race snacks on Saturday. Shops inside the Hauptbahnhof are the usual exception when you forget something.

Traffic in Jakarta is the real opening act. Trips take far longer than the map suggests, especially on Friday.
The main options:

- **MRT Jakarta:** the North–South line runs from Lebak Bulus to Bundaran HI along Jalan Sudirman and Jalan Thamrin. It is the fastest way through the central business corridor for venues near it.
- **TransJakarta:** the busway network has dedicated lanes on main roads. It is cheap and wide-reaching, but crowded at rush hour.
- **KRL Commuterline:** the suburban rail network is useful for venues out in satellite cities such as Tangerang.
- **Grab and Gojek:** ride-hailing cars and motorbike taxis (*ojek*) are everywhere. A motorbike slips through jams that hold cars still.

After a big concert, thousands of people open the same apps at once. Prices surge and drivers struggle to reach the gates. Walking ten minutes away from the venue before requesting a ride usually means a quicker pickup.
Late October sits at the turn into Jakarta's wet season, and heavy evening downpours are common. A light rain jacket is easier than a soaked commute home.
Indonesian concerts have their own routine at the gate, and knowing it makes the queue less stressful.

- **ID that matches the ticket.** Local promoters commonly tie tickets to the buyer's name and check identification at redemption or entry. Foreign visitors use a passport.
- **Wristband exchange.** Many Jakarta shows swap e-tickets for wristbands at a redemption booth, sometimes on a separate day or at a separate time.
- **Digital payment.** Merch stands and food vendors at Jakarta events generally take QRIS codes and e-wallets such as GoPay, OVO and DANA. Many also take cards. Some rupiah in cash helps when a signal drops.
- **Bag rules.** Promoters usually restrict large bags, professional cameras and outside food and drink.

On the floor, Jakarta crowds typically sing every word, loudly and in English. Standing-area fans queue early for barrier spots. An area near the sound desk usually gives a clear view with more elbow room.

LANY's catalogue rewards fans who know the early records. "ILYSB" is the one Indonesian crowds sing first. Its looping synth hook and short title made it a lasting favourite with Indonesian listeners.

"Malibu Nights" goes the other way: slow, piano-led and heartbroken. It is the kind of song where phone torches come up across an arena. Frontman Paul Klein has a habit of talking to the crowd between songs, often pausing to address the city directly.
The setlist was not fixed in advance. Fans following the tour through earlier Asian stops were the quickest guide to what the band was playing on this leg.
Jakarta's street food runs late, and the areas around big venues usually fill with carts and warung stalls on show nights. Nasi goreng, sate ayam and martabak are the staples.
For anyone staying over, a hotel on the same side of the city as the venue means a short ride back at midnight rather than a long one through Jakarta's toll roads.
